section.title: Triumph in Christ
section.sectionRationale: Breaking off his travel narrative at the anxious moment when he could not find Titus, Paul erupts into thanksgiving. He pictures God leading him in a Roman triumphal procession, always in Christ, and through him spreading everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of God. That fragrance is the aroma of Christ, life to those being saved and death to those perishing. Overwhelmed by the weight of such a ministry, Paul asks who is sufficient for it, and answers that unlike the many who peddle God's word, he speaks with sincerity, as a man sent from God.
section.thesis: God always leads His servants in Christ's triumphal procession, spreading through them the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, an aroma of life to the saved and death to the perishing; and only those who speak God's word with sincerity, as men sent from God rather than peddlers for profit, are equal to so weighty a task.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the open door at Troas and Paul's restless search for Titus that drove him on to Macedonia; and the great thanksgiving for triumph in Christ, the aroma of Christ that means life or death, and the sincerity of true ministry against those who peddle God's word.

units.label: An open door but no peace
units.note: restless without Titus, on to Macedonia

verses.text: Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord,
I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

units.label: Triumph in Christ and the aroma of life or death
units.note: led as captives, the fragrance of the knowledge of Him

verses.text: But thanks be to God, who always {{thriambeuo|leads us triumphantly}} as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the {{euodia|fragrance}} of the knowledge of Him.
For we are to God the sweet {{osme|aroma}} of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing.
To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life. And who is qualified for such a task?
For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God.

thriambeuo.gloss: To lead in a triumphal procession. The image is the Roman triumph, the lavish victory parade in which a conquering general displayed his captives before the crowds. Strikingly, Paul casts himself not as the victor but among the captives led along in Christ's train, conquered by grace and put on display for God's glory. The word turns apparent weakness into triumph: to be led captive by Christ is to share in His victory and to make His conquest known everywhere.

euodia.gloss: A sweet smell, a fragrance, a pleasing aroma. In the Old Testament it describes the pleasing aroma of sacrifices that ascend to God. Paul says God spreads through His servants the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, so that the gospel is like a perfume filling every place. The ministry of the gospel is not merely heard but sensed, a pleasing aroma to God Himself, carried through the world by those who make Christ known.

osme.gloss: A smell or odor, whether pleasant or repugnant depending on the one who perceives it. Paul says believers are the aroma of Christ, and the same gospel scent is life giving to those being saved and deathly to those perishing. The image may recall the Roman triumph, where the incense of the parade meant celebration to the victors but doom to the captives bound for execution. The gospel is never neutral; the same message divides its hearers.

basic.context: Paul had come to Troas to preach, and the Lord opened a real door for the gospel there. Yet his anxiety over the Corinthians, and the absence of Titus who was to bring news of them, gave him no rest, so he pressed on to Macedonia. Then, thinking of God's faithfulness, he bursts into thanksgiving: God always leads him in Christ's triumphal procession and spreads through him the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, a fragrance that means life to some and death to others.
basic.hermeneutics: The abrupt shift from travel report to thanksgiving shows how Paul's mind runs to Christ even in distress. Read the triumph image against the Roman victory parade, where captives were displayed. Paul places himself among the captives led by Christ, not the conqueror. Verses 15 and 16 teach that the gospel is never neutral, and verse 17 contrasts sincere ministry with peddling God's word.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul thanks God who thriambeuo, leads him in triumphal procession, the Roman victory parade, as one of Christ's captives. Through him God spreads the euodia, the sweet fragrance, of the knowledge of Christ. Believers are the osme, the aroma, of Christ, a scent that means life to the saved and death to the perishing.
basic.typology: The fragrance language echoes the pleasing aroma of Old Testament sacrifices that ascended to God. The ministry of the gospel, and the lives of those who carry it, rise to God as a pleasing aroma because they are the aroma of Christ, the true and final sacrifice.
basic.christ: Everything here is in Christ. It is Christ's triumph in which Paul is led, the knowledge of Christ that spreads as fragrance, and the aroma of Christ that believers become. The victory celebrated is Christ's conquest of sin and death, and the ministry is nothing less than making Christ known to a watching world.
basic.god: God is the one who always leads His servants in triumph and spreads the knowledge of Christ through them. He is the God to whom the aroma is pleasing, before whom Paul speaks with sincerity. He is sovereign over the outcome, using the same gospel for salvation and for judgment, and He commissions and sends His true ministers.
basic.crossReferences: Colossians 2 shows Christ triumphing over the powers, disarming and displaying them. 1 Corinthians 1 says the message of the cross is folly to those perishing but power to those being saved. Ephesians 5 speaks of Christ's self offering as a fragrant aroma to God. 2 Corinthians 4 continues the theme of open, sincere ministry.
basic.oneStory: The Bible is the story of God's victory in Christ over sin and death, and of that victory being made known through His people. Paul, led as a captive in Christ's triumph, carries the fragrance of Christ everywhere, a fragrance that saves and judges. The whole mission of the church is here in miniature: to make Christ known, in sincerity, as those sent by God.

context.literary:
Paul stops his travel story in mid sentence. Verse 13 leaves him on the road to Macedonia with Titus still missing, and the account is not picked up again until 2 Corinthians 7:5-7, where Titus finally arrives with good news. Everything between those two points, nearly five chapters, is a long digression on what gospel ministry is and what it costs. The thanksgiving of verse 14 is the first note of that digression, so the break is not a lapse of memory. It is the author deciding that the real story of his journey is not the route but the God who leads.

Verses 14 to 17 build in a clear sequence. A thanksgiving sentence in verse 14 holds two claims joined by 'and': God leads us, and God spreads the fragrance through us. Verse 15 names the fragrance, verse 16 splits it into two effects, and then a question breaks the flow, 'And who is qualified for such a task?' Verse 17 answers by contrast, 'we are not like so many others.' The sentence runs from praise to a stunned question to a defence, which is exactly how Paul argues when he feels the weight of what he has said.

The question of verse 16 is picked up almost word for word in 3:5-6, where Paul says the competence comes from God, and the 'sincerity' and 'peddle' of verse 17 are answered again in 4:2, where he refuses to 'distort the word of God.' The passage works as an overture. It states in a few lines the themes the next chapters will develop: Christ's triumph, the double effect of the message, and a ministry that is accountable to God before it is accountable to anyone in Corinth.
context.historical:
Troas was a harbour city on the north west coast of what is now Turkey, a Roman colony and a natural gateway between Asia and Macedonia. Paul had been there before. It was at Troas that he saw the vision of the man of Macedonia, Acts 16:8-10, and he would stay there again for a week on his last journey, Acts 20:5-8. In this visit he found an open door, a phrase he uses of real opportunity elsewhere in 1 Corinthians 16:9, and walked away from it because he could not find Titus. A modern reader may find that startling. Paul places his love for a struggling church above a ready harvest.

Behind all this lies the strained relationship with Corinth. Titus had been sent to carry the severe letter Paul describes in 2:1-4, written through many tears, and Paul was waiting to learn how the church had taken it. His anxiety was the anxiety of a pastor who might have wounded people he loved.

The image of verse 14 comes from the Roman triumph, the grandest public ceremony the city knew. A victorious general rode in procession through the streets with his army, the plunder of the war, and the captured leaders walking in chains. Incense was burned along the route in honour of the gods. To the soldiers and the crowd the smell meant victory and festival. To the prisoners, many of whom were put to death at the end of the day, it meant the end of their lives. Paul's first readers, in a city that was itself a Roman colony, knew this picture well. They also knew the second image, the travelling teacher who sold wisdom for money, a figure common in the Greek cities and the target of verse 17.
context.canonical:
The fragrance language reaches back to the beginning of Israel's worship. After the flood Noah's offering is received as a pleasing aroma, Genesis 8:21, and the burnt offerings of the Law are described the same way, Exodus 29:18. Paul has given this old vocabulary a new subject. The sweet smell that rose from the altar now rises from a person, and it is the aroma of Christ himself. Later he will use the same words of the Philippians' gift to him, Philippians 4:18, and of Christ's own self offering, Ephesians 5:2, so that the sacrifice, the gift and the life of the believer are all taken into one picture.

The double effect of the message has deep roots in the prophets. God sent Isaiah to a people who would hear and not understand, Isaiah 6:9-10, and Simeon told Mary that her child would cause the rise and fall of many, Luke 2:34. Peter says the same stone is precious to those who believe and a stone of stumbling to those who do not, 1 Peter 2:7-8. Paul stands in that line. The message does not change from hearer to hearer; the hearers differ.

The triumph picture is taken up in Colossians 2:15, where Christ himself is the one who triumphs over the powers by the cross, and in Ephesians 4:8, which applies Psalm 68:18 to the ascended Lord leading captives. Verse 17 stands against a long prophetic complaint about teachers who sell what is not theirs to sell, Micah 3:11, and finds its New Testament echo in Paul's own defence in 1 Thessalonians 2:3-5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is not simply reporting why his plans changed. He is teaching the Corinthians how to read his life. They had questioned his reliability and his credentials, and some of them measured a minister by polish, letters of recommendation and success. Paul replies by changing the standard. If he is a captive in Christ's procession, then his weakness, his restlessness at Troas and even the opposition he meets are not signs that God has abandoned him. They are the shape that victory takes in this age.

He also wants them to feel the seriousness of the message. A word that carries life and death is not to be handled lightly or shaped to please the hearers. The question 'who is qualified?' is not a modest flourish; it is a real recognition that no human being is fit to bear such a word. The answer the letter will give is that qualification comes from God, 3:5. Meanwhile Paul asks his readers to examine the other teachers by a simple test, whether they speak as people sent from God and before God, or as traders making a living from his word.

Finally the passage is a gentle appeal. By turning his anxiety about Titus into thanksgiving, Paul shows the Corinthians what he hopes for them: a faith that can bring even a troubled and unfinished moment before God and find him already at work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The story of Troas is description. Paul had an open door and moved on because he could not settle without news of Titus. Nothing in the text turns that into a rule that ministers should leave fruitful work whenever they are anxious. Paul's choice is recorded honestly, and he does not present it as a model, only as a fact the Corinthians need in order to understand him.

The triumph is also a description of what God does, not a task for believers to carry out. The verbs of verse 14 have God as their subject: he leads and he spreads. The believer's part is to be carried along and to speak truthfully. That frees the reader from a mistaken application in which the aroma has to be manufactured by effort, charm or technique.

What does bind us is the contrast of verse 17. Handling God's word for profit or with a hidden agenda is wrong, and sincerity before God is a standing requirement for everyone who teaches or speaks for him. It also protects against a careless reading of verse 16. Paul is not telling anyone to be content with offending people or to take pride in a hostile response. The 'odor of death' is what happens when the true gospel is rejected, not a goal to aim for.

debates.question: In the triumphal procession, are believers the victors or the led captives?

views.label: Led as captives in Christ's triumph
views.case: The verb thriambeuo normally means to lead someone as a conquered captive in a triumph, so Paul pictures himself as one taken captive by Christ and displayed in His victory parade, a striking image of strength through surrender that suits the letter's theme of power in weakness.

views.label: Led in triumph as sharers in the victory
views.case: Some render it that God causes us to triumph or leads us in triumph as participants in Christ's conquest, stressing that believers share in His victory rather than being merely his prisoners.

debates.bearing: The grammar favors the captive image, and it fits Paul's gospel of glory through weakness; either way the triumph belongs to Christ, and to be led by Him is to share in and display His conquest.

debates.question: What is the background of the fragrance and aroma imagery?

views.label: The incense of the Roman triumph
views.case: The scent that meant celebration to victors and death to condemned captives fits the triumphal procession just described, so the aroma of life and death continues the parade image with vivid force.

views.label: The pleasing aroma of Old Testament sacrifice
views.case: The word euodia is used in the Greek Old Testament for the pleasing aroma of sacrifices to God, suggesting that Paul sees the gospel and the lives of its ministers as a fragrant offering ascending to God.

debates.bearing: The two backgrounds are not exclusive; the triumph supplies the immediate picture while the sacrificial overtone deepens it, so that the gospel is both the scent of Christ's victory and a pleasing offering to God.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb thriambeuo in verse 14 is rare. In the New Testament it appears here and in Colossians 2:15, where the same word describes Christ triumphing over the powers. Translators have to decide whether it means 'leads us in triumph' as the victors, or 'leads us as captives in a triumphal procession.' The BSB gives 'leads us triumphantly as captives.' Two things favour the captive reading. A Roman triumph had a defined place for the conquered, and Paul's whole defence of himself in this letter rests on weakness. The reading also fits 4:10, where he carries about the death of Jesus in his body. Yet verse 14 also has a strong note of thanks and victory, so the image holds both sides: the one led is a prisoner and also a sharer in the celebration because the conqueror is his Lord.

Two Greek words for smell are in play and are worth keeping apart. Osme is the general word for odour or scent, and it is what spreads 'everywhere' in verse 14 and what the message is to its two kinds of hearer in verse 16. Euodia, 'sweet aroma' in verse 15, is the word for a good smell, and it is what Paul says the ministers are 'to God.' The two words stand together in Ephesians 5:2 and Philippians 4:18, where the same pairing describes an offering received by God. So in verse 15 the first direction of the fragrance is upward, to God, and only then outward to the people among whom it is released.

The ending of verse 16 is compressed in Greek. Literally, the aroma is 'out of death into death' for some and 'out of life into life' for others. The repeated pattern suggests a direction of travel: the message leads those who reject it from death further into death, and those who receive it from life into fuller life. The BSB's 'odor of death and demise' and 'fragrance that brings life' catch the result but lose the sense of movement.

The verb kapeleuo, 'peddle' in verse 17, comes from kapelos, the word for a retail dealer or huckster. The noun carried an old reputation for dishonest dealing, the shopkeeper who dilutes his goods to improve his profit. Paul accuses the other teachers of watering down or trading in the word of God. Against this he sets eilikrineia, 'sincerity.' The word is also used in 1 Corinthians 5:8 and 2 Corinthians 1:12, and describes something that holds up under examination. Paul speaks 'in Christ' and 'before God,' which means he is willing to be examined at God's own bar.

Finally the question 'who is qualified?' uses the adjective hikanos, which means sufficient, fit or adequate. Its related forms return in 3:5-6, where Paul says that God has made us competent. The question of 2:16 is the setup, and 3:5 is the answer.

typology.type: The pleasing aroma of the burnt offering, Genesis 8:21 and Exodus 29:18
typology.fulfillment: In the Law the smell of the offering rising from the altar was how Scripture pictured God accepting a gift. Paul says that the aroma is now Christ himself, and that his servants share in it because they are in him, 2:15. The final correspondence is Ephesians 5:2, where Christ gives himself up as a fragrant sacrificial offering. The old sacrifices were repeated, but Christ's offering was once for all, Hebrews 10:12. The type also falls short in this: the animal had no choice, while Christ gave himself willingly.

typology.type: The captives led in a conqueror's procession, Psalm 68:18
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a victor leading captives is older than Rome. Psalm 68:18 praises the LORD for ascending on high and leading captives away, and Paul reads that verse of the ascended Christ in Ephesians 4:8. In 2 Corinthians 2:14 he places himself in the procession. Where the pagan captive was led to be shamed and killed, Paul is led to be displayed as the trophy of grace: a persecutor made into a minister, 1 Timothy 1:13-16. The type breaks at this point, since the conqueror's prisoners are not ordinarily given a share in his triumph.

Aaron was to burn incense on the golden altar every morning and evening, and the cloud of fragrance rose before the veil. The smoke carries the people's prayers in Revelation 8:3-4 and in Luke 1:9-10, where the crowd prays while Zechariah burns incense. Paul takes the sanctuary scent and sends it through the Mediterranean world. The fragrance of the knowledge of Christ is no longer shut inside a tent. The type is also stretched: incense was fragrant for all who stood near it, but the aroma of Christ divides, giving life to some and death to others.

typology.type: The pillar that led Israel, Exodus 13:21
typology.fulfillment: God went before his people in the wilderness, in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and they followed where he led. Paul speaks of the same leading, with the pillar replaced by Christ's triumph: God 'always leads us.' The word 'always' makes the leading continuous, including at Troas where Paul felt lost. The pillar was a visible sign, and now the leading is known by faith, Romans 8:14. The correspondence is of kind, not of detail, and Paul does not claim that the pillar was literally a picture of the triumph.

study.christ:
The first thing to see is how much of this passage is simply 'in Christ.' Paul preached 'the gospel of Christ' at Troas, verse 12. God leads him 'in Christ,' verse 14. He knows the fragrance as 'the knowledge of Him,' and he is 'the sweet aroma of Christ,' verse 15. He speaks 'in Christ,' verse 17. Everything Paul calls his ministry is located in a person, not in a method.

The picture of triumph points to Christ in two ways. He is the one whose victory is celebrated. The cross, which looked like defeat to Rome, was the place where he disarmed the powers and made a public spectacle of them, Colossians 2:15. The Greek word for triumph in that verse is the same word Paul uses here, and the two texts explain each other. The procession Paul walks in is the procession of the crucified and risen Lord. It is also true that Christ is the pattern of the captive. He was led away, Isaiah 53:7, and he gave himself up as a fragrant offering, Ephesians 5:2. When Paul describes himself as a person carried along by someone else's victory, he is being conformed to the one who gave himself up.

The aroma points to Christ as the one who divides. Simeon said the child was appointed for the rise and fall of many, Luke 2:34, and Jesus himself said that he came so that those who do not see would see, and those who see would become blind, John 9:39. Peter writes that he is the cornerstone for those who believe and a stumbling stone for those who do not, 1 Peter 2:7-8. A message about Christ is never neutral because Christ is not neutral. People meet either life or death in him, and they cannot stand beside him without a response.

It also points to Christ in the question 'who is qualified?' Paul does not answer by pointing at himself. He will say that the sufficiency is from God, 3:5, and by the time we reach 4:5 he says plainly, 'we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord.' The fragrance that spreads through him is not his character, his gifts or his oratory. It is the knowledge of Christ.

A last link concerns the word 'sent.' Paul claims to speak as one sent from God, verse 17, and the same pattern of sending runs through the Gospels, where Jesus is the one sent by the Father, John 20:21. The ministers of the new covenant carry the Sent One's own errand.

Caution is wise with the picture. The aroma does not mean that Christ is somehow harmful, and Paul is not saying that rejection is the plan for the people concerned. The text tells us what happens to the message, and elsewhere Paul grieves over those who refuse it, Romans 9:1-3. The triumph is Christ's, and the mercy that leads captives is his as well.
study.god:
Several things appear about God in these six verses. The first is that he is the subject of the sentence. Paul has been in a state of unrest, with no peace in his spirit, and then writes 'thanks be to God.' The verbs of verse 14 are God's: he leads, he spreads, he makes the knowledge known. This is a God who is working in the middle of a failed errand, a missing friend and a restless apostle. The failed visit to Troas does not mean that something has slipped out of his hands.

He is a God of triumph, and his triumph is real. The powers that oppose the gospel have been disarmed, Colossians 2:15. Paul's lot as a captive does not contradict this, because the same God who leads him as a captive has defeated the powers that held him once. He does not need Paul's strength to win. This gives believers a firm basis for hope when the work looks like failure.

God is also the one who chooses to work through persons. The fragrance spreads 'through us,' and 'everywhere.' He is not content to broadcast the knowledge of himself in a way that needs no human voices. The preacher, the friend, the writer and the visitor are the vessels. This links with 4:7, where the treasure is in jars of clay, and it shows God's humility as well as his power.

The passage shows a God of justice and mercy held together. The same message produces two results, and God does not set one hearer's life against another's. The text does not say that death is what God wants for those who perish; elsewhere Scripture says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11, and wishes that all would come to repentance, 2 Peter 3:9. Nor does Paul settle the tension by weakening either side. The word divides, and God is in the dividing.

God is the one before whom Paul speaks, verse 17. That means he is a witness and a judge, and the sincerity he asks for is the sincerity of someone who knows the Lord is listening. Paul's confidence in this letter does not rest on the Corinthians' approval but on God's examination of his heart, 1 Thessalonians 2:4. A God who examines hearts both comforts the honest and warns the peddler.

For worship, the passage teaches thanksgiving before resolution. Paul praises God before he has heard from Titus, and in the next chapters we will see that the news came and his joy was restored, 7:6-7. Worship that waits until problems are solved misses the gift of this passage, which is that God is worthy of thanks while the road is still unclear.

crossReferences.note: The only other New Testament use of the verb for triumphing. There Christ is the conqueror who disarms the powers and displays them by the cross. Set beside 2 Corinthians 2:14, it shows that the procession Paul walks in is the victory parade of the crucified Lord, not of a human general.

Troas is where Paul first received the call to Macedonia. When he returns to the same city in 2 Corinthians 2:12-13 and again heads for Macedonia, the reader sees that the geography of his ministry has been shaped by God from the start, even when it looks like restless wandering.

The resumption of the story broken off at 2:13. Paul arrives in Macedonia, is pressed by fears within, and then God comforts him through the arrival of Titus. The long digression between the two passages is bracketed by this reunion, and the thanksgiving of 2:14 is shown to be justified.

Christ gave himself up as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God. It supplies the background of Paul's phrase 'the sweet aroma of Christ.' Believers are told to walk in love in the same way, so the fragrance that rises to God is a life shaped by his self giving.

Paul calls the Philippians' gift a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God. The word picture shows that the aroma language is not reserved for apostles. Any act of faithful generosity or service can be a sacrifice God receives gladly.

Written earlier to this same church, it states the same division with a different image: the cross is folly to one group and God's power to the other. Paul uses both pairs of words, perishing and being saved, so he is plainly teaching one consistent account of how the gospel is received.

Simeon's word to Mary that the child is appointed for the rise and fall of many in Israel is the Gospel counterpart of the aroma of life and death. Both texts say that Christ forces a decision and that people cannot treat him as one more subject of opinion.

The prophet condemns priests who teach for a price and prophets who divine for money while insisting that the LORD is among them. It is the Old Testament background to peddling God's word, and it shows that Paul's complaint in verse 17 repeats a long prophetic charge.

Paul's earlier statement of the same standard: no deceit, no flattery, no pretext for greed, speaking as those approved by God and examined by God. It shows that sincerity before God was a settled conviction long before the Corinthian conflict forced him to defend it.

The answer to the question left hanging in 2:16. Competence does not come from ourselves but from God, who qualifies ministers of a new covenant. The two passages should be read together, since the question and the answer frame everything Paul says about the glory and cost of the ministry.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with God as the one who goes out to meet his creatures. He walks in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and leads Israel by a pillar, Exodus 13:21. This passage sits in the same story. Paul has been through anxiety and a closed hope, and he says that God is still leading. The story of redemption is not mainly a story of human searching, and the Troas passage shows a man who is searching and being led at the same time.

The passage also answers a question that grows out of the whole Old Testament: what happens when God's powers meet the powers that oppose him? The exodus was a triumph, with Pharaoh's army overthrown, Exodus 15:1-4, and the Psalms sing of a conqueror who ascends with captives. Colossians 2:15 says the decisive victory has been won at the cross. Paul's procession is the aftermath of that battle, in which the gospel is carried through the world as the proclamation of a won war.

Looking back, the sweet aroma of the sacrifices from Noah's altar to the tabernacle was a promise that God would receive an offering that actually satisfied him. In Christ that promise is kept. Looking forward, the line that runs from the first Christians to the present is the same fragrance, spread through ordinary people in ordinary places. Every church, every conversation about Jesus and every act of faithful service adds to it. The division the passage describes is also not final, because the Bible's last chapters show those who are being saved and those who are perishing gathered into two destinies, Revelation 22:14-15.

The story ends in a world where the knowledge of the LORD covers the earth as the waters cover the sea, Isaiah 11:9, and where the procession of the nations brings their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24-26. What Paul experiences as a thin thread of fragrance in Asia Minor and Macedonia will fill the new creation. The captive led in Christ's triumph will take part in the victory feast of the One who led him.

quiz.q: What image does Paul use to describe how God leads His servants?

options.text: A triumphal procession, in which he is led as a captive in Christ's victory.
options.note: The verb pictures the Roman triumph, with Paul among Christ's captives on display.

options.text: A victorious general leading his own troops to conquest.
options.note: The triumph is Christ's; Paul is led in it, not the conquering general himself.

options.text: A quiet walk with no hardship along the way.
options.note: Paul had just described real anxiety; the triumph is Christ's amid Paul's weakness.

options.text: A retreat from a battle already lost.
options.note: It is a victory parade, celebrating Christ's conquest, not a defeat.

quiz.q: What does Paul say the gospel is to those who hear it?

options.text: The aroma of Christ, life to those being saved and death to those perishing.
options.note: Verses 15 and 16 show the same gospel dividing its hearers.

options.text: A message that everyone eventually accepts.
options.note: The gospel is offered to all, but it is received as life by some and death by others.

options.text: A private matter with no effect on those who reject it.
options.note: The gospel is never neutral; to the perishing it is an odor of death.

options.text: A fragrance pleasing only to those who already believe.
options.note: It is pleasing to God, and its effect reaches saved and perishing alike.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe his own ministry in contrast to others?

options.text: He speaks with sincerity, as a man sent from God, not peddling the word for profit.
options.note: Verse 17 contrasts sincere, God sent ministry with peddling God's word.

options.text: He preaches more skillfully than the others.
options.note: The contrast is sincerity and calling, not superior eloquence.

options.text: He charges a fair price for his teaching.
options.note: Paul rejects making profit from God's word, not merely overcharging.

options.text: He keeps the gospel to a small, worthy circle.
options.note: Paul spreads the fragrance everywhere; he does not restrict it.

quiz.q: Why did Paul leave Troas even though a door for the gospel stood open?

options.text: He had no peace because Titus was not there, so he went on to Macedonia.
options.note: Verse 13 gives his restlessness over Titus as the reason.

options.text: The people there refused to listen to him.
options.note: The door was open; the issue was his anxiety, not rejection.

options.text: God told him to stop preaching in Troas.
options.note: The text names his lack of peace over Titus, not a divine prohibition.

options.text: He had lost interest in preaching the gospel.
options.note: Paul came precisely to preach; his heart for the gospel never wavered.

questions: Paul turned a moment of deep anxiety into thanksgiving for God's triumph in Christ. What present worry could you bring before God and answer with thanks for His certain victory?
To be led as a captive in Christ's triumph is to find strength through surrender. Where is God calling you to be conquered by His grace rather than trusting your own strength?
You are called to be the aroma of Christ wherever you go. What fragrance is your life spreading among those who do not yet know Him?
The same gospel is life to some and death to others. How does this sober truth shape the way you share Christ, and free you from measuring success only by results?
Paul refused to peddle God's word for profit and spoke with sincerity before God. In your service and speech, are you seeking your own gain or ministering as one sent from God?

translationNotes.note: Leads us triumphantly as captives renders thriambeuo, to lead in a triumphal procession; the verb normally pictures conquered captives displayed in a Roman triumph, so Paul casts himself among Christ's captives, led in His victory.

The BSB footnote gives the literal sense as an aroma from death to death and an aroma from life to life; the doubled phrases stress how completely the gospel affects its hearers for death or for life.

Peddle the word of God renders a verb for trading or hawking goods for profit, often with a hint of adulterating the product; Paul contrasts such profiteering with speaking sincerely as one sent from God.
